title: Kavyamimamsa Builds an Empire of Words

title_i18n.en: Kavyamimamsa Builds an Empire of Words

subtitle: How Rājaśekhara Measured the World with Poetry
era: Literary theory at and after Kannauj, c. 900-930 CE
region: Kannauj and the mapped Sanskrit world
moral: A civilization endures when it studies how creation works.

sources.citation: Rajashekhara, Kavyamimamsa, ed. C.D. Dalal and R.A. Shastry (1916); trans. Sadhana Parashar (2000)
sources.note: Primary treatise on poetics, geography, education and literary ethics.

sources.citation: Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (2006)
sources.note: Places the text in the Sanskrit cosmopolitan order.

sources.citation: Siegfried Lienhard, A History of Classical Poetry: Sanskrit, Pali, Prakrit (1984)

panels.shot: epic low-angle wide inside a lamplit royal library

dialogue.text: In Gurjara-Pratihara Kannauj, court poet Rājaśekhara dared to ask: can poetry become a science of the world—and will that science outlive the empire that sponsors it?

panels.shot: slow push-in from balcony down to bustling city and palace complex

dialogue.text: Around 900 CE, Kannauj is a beating heart of power. Under the Gurjara-Pratiharas, it draws merchants, monks and poets from across the Sanskrit world into its stone and dust.

panels.shot: medium interior shot in royal hall with king off-frame, focus on the poet

dialogue.text: Rājaśekhara serves at court, praised for drama and verse. But in his study he begins a different work—a treatise on how poetry itself is made, taught and judged.

panels.shot: intimate close-up of hands and manuscript on a low desk

dialogue.text: He calls it Kavyamimamsa—an inquiry into poetry. Not just rules, but a map of inspiration, training, beauty, fault, borrowing, and even the lands where poets work.

panels.shot: slow push-in to Rājaśekhara seated with young disciples

dialogue.text: In its surviving chapters, he speaks directly to students of poetry: how to be trained, how to recognize faults and excellences, how to discipline feeling into form.

panels.shot: close-up on his face, eyes lifted as if receiving a distant voice

dialogue.text: He writes of poetic inspiration as something both mysterious and trainable—an inner wind that must be guided by study, practice and attention to earlier masters.

panels.shot: medium shot with two students reciting while he listens

dialogue.text: He catalogs faults: forced metaphors, clumsy sound, misplaced emotion. And he identifies beauties—suggestion, grace, precision—teaching how to hear quality, not just cleverness.

panels.shot: low, thoughtful angle as he pulls out older manuscripts

dialogue.text: But he knows no poem is born in emptiness. In one chapter he turns to borrowing—how new poets may take from old works without merely copying them.

panels.shot: diagrammatic overhead shot of manuscripts radiating out around him

dialogue.text: He distinguishes kinds of reuse—echo, transformation, close following—and judges them on artistry. Skillful borrowing becomes homage; lazy repetition, a fault.

panels.shot: medium shot with him addressing a skeptical student

dialogue.speaker: rajashekhara
dialogue.text: We live among other poets’ words. The test is not escape, but how we reshape them.

panels.shot: slow pull-back to reveal wall-hanging map and manuscripts

dialogue.text: Then his inquiry shifts. He unrolls a bhuvanakosha—a cosmography. He begins to list regions, rivers, and cities, building a world-picture around Kannauj.

panels.shot: close-up on the map with his finger tracing routes

dialogue.text: This geography is not idle curiosity. It shows where Sanskrit learning lives—linking distant courts and temples into one imagined scholarly world.

panels.shot: wide shot of court hall with map displayed before nobles

dialogue.text: For a king of Kannauj, such a map carries quiet power. To name regions and centres of learning is to imagine an imperial reach over culture, not only over armies.

panels.shot: medium shot of him shelving his manuscript among others

dialogue.text: We do not have the full design of his work; only part of a larger project survives. Yet even in fragments we see a single ambition—to order the craft of culture.

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide: fading from lively court to dim, quiet ruins

dialogue.text: The Gurjara-Pratihara state would weaken and fragment. The stone halls fell silent. Yet the palm leaves bearing Kavyamimamsa traveled beyond Kannauj’s decline.

panels.shot: montage-style wide of different later scholars with the same manuscript

dialogue.text: Centuries later, critics and poets would still read him. Modern editors and translators study his treatise to understand how the Sanskrit cosmopolitan order saw itself.

panels.shot: extreme close-up on manuscript leaf, inked title Kavyamimamsa

dialogue.text: In these pages, poetry is not mere ornament. It becomes a way to think about borrowing, training, geography—a method for studying how creation itself works.

panels.shot: final contemplative wide shot of Rājaśekhara silhouetted against the city and sky

dialogue.text: Rājaśekhara’s empire was built of words, maps and measures. When stone kingdoms crumble, such empires endure wherever people still ask how culture is made, and how it should be judged.
